title: Glacial warmup observations and sparse-QPS replay
content:
Context:
This is a scratchpad for a very slow, low-frequency traffic pattern we call 'glacial warmup' — essentially long idle windows (minutes-hours) with sporadic single requests. Goal: understand tail behavior, first-token penalty, and effectiveness of small persistent caches (prefix and KV) when arrivals are extremely sparse.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Production customer (internal simulation) expects 0.01 qps steady with occasional small bursts (<5 rps for <30s).
- Existing heuristics (aggressive cache eviction after 30s idle) may be causing repeated first-token penalties and model cold-starts inside the serving process.
- Need to quantify: how much cost (latency + token overhead) comes from these repeated warmups vs keeping a tiny hot pool or sticky KV cache entries.

Environment / setup:
- Model: redwood-6B-quant (Representative internal variant; inference config ~= 4-bit quantized weights).
- Hardware: Dedicated T4-small pool (2 GPUs), single instance used for runs.
- Runtime: commit runtime@main 2026-02-10 (PR 987 contains small batching tweak).
- Harness: custom replay harness (python) that issues single requests at configured intervals; instruments first-token, last-token, and total tokens produced. Measurements recorded to CSV.
- KV cache TTL tested: 15s (baseline), 60s, 300s, and infinite (manual).
- Sticky worker policy: off vs sticky=1 (pin tenant to same worker for 10m).

Test matrix (high level):
- Scenario A: 1 request every 30s for 6 hours (glacial-30s).
- Scenario B: 1 request every 5 minutes for 24 hours (glacial-5m).
- Scenario C: diurnal micro burst: 10 requests at t=0 then back to 5-min cadence (burst+glacial).
- Each scenario repeated under KV TTLs [15s, 60s, 300s, inf] and sticky on/off.
- Measured: first_token_latency_ms, p50/p95/p99 of total response latency, cold_cache_indicator (boolean when cache miss on prefix), model_tokens_generated (to detect re-tokenization), and estimated extra GPU time (ms).

Representative raw numbers (selected):
- Baseline KV TTL=15s, sticky=off, scenario A (1 req /30s):
  * run length: 6h (720 requests)
  * first_token_latency_ms: mean=520, p95=1280, p99=2560
  * cold_cache_indicator: ~68% of requests flagged as cache-miss (roughly matches 30s TTL)
  * extra model tokens per miss (est): +12 tokens on average (due to repeated prompt re-encode overhead)
  * observed downstream user-perceived P95 spikes coincide with misses.

- KV TTL=60s, sticky=off, scenario A:
  * first_token_latency_ms: mean=410, p95=950, p99=1700
  * cold_cache_indicator: ~35%
  * cost: roughly 30% lower GPU time wasted vs baseline.

- KV TTL=300s, sticky=off, scenario A:
  * first_token_latency_ms: mean=360, p95=720, p99=1200
  * cold_cache_indicator: ~12%
  * tradeoff: memory usage per tenant went up ~+8KB per cached prefix entry (small).

- KV TTL=60s, sticky=on, scenario A:
  * first_token_latency_ms: mean=330, p95=700, p99=1100
  * cold_cache_indicator: ~8% (sticky ensures next request hits same worker and benefits from in-process prefix cache)
  * but observed small contention when tenant stuck on a worker under peak background (work-stealing reduced throughput by ~4%).

- Scenario B (1 per 5m) with KV TTL=300s:
  * cold_cache_indicator: ~94% (requests spaced longer than TTL) -> meaning TTL must be >300s to be effective for 5-min pattern; infinite TTL helped but memory accumulation risk.

- Scenario C (burst then glacial), KV TTL=60s:
  * Burst part had excellent latencies (p50 < 120ms). After burst, cold-cache misses increased as TTL expired; next 10 sparse requests incurring p95 spikes similar to baseline.

Observations / interpretation:
- Short TTL (15s) is catastrophically bad for glacial patterns: repeated first-token penalties dominate P95/P99 even though average QPS is low.
- A modest TTL (60-300s) dramatically reduces miss rate and P95; returns diminish beyond 300s for 30s cadence but matter for 5-min cadences.
- Sticky worker policy helps but introduces fairness/throughput side effects when workers get pinned to noisy tenants. Should be optional and bounded (e.g., stickiness window with eviction heuristics).
- Memory footprint for prefix/KV entries is small per tenant; the main operational risk is unbounded retention in infinite-TTL case for thousands of tenants.

Quick calculations (cost perspective):
- Estimate: each cache-miss costs ~+0.35s of GPU time (first-token overhead) => at $X per GPU-second (placeholder), repeated misses matter even at low qps.
- For 1 req /30s, with 68% misses and 720 reqs, wasted GPU time ~720 * 0.68 * 0.35s = ~171s over 6 hours per tenant. If scaled to 1k tenants with similar pattern, becomes material.

Anomalies / data quality notes:
- A couple of p99 spikes correlated with background serializer GC on the worker (not pure model warmup). Need to run a second pass with tracing enabled to separate worker GC vs model kernel cold paths.
- Some requests showed huge first-token latencies (~6s) but accompanying logs showed transient GPU throttling (OOM killer attempts) — these runs should be excluded from summary.

Immediate small experiments to run next (prioritized):
1) TTL auto-tuning: test adaptive TTL based on inter-arrival distribution estimate per tenant (e.g., keep until 3x median interarrival).  A/B run vs static 60s.
2) Sticky-lite: pin for 60s only and allow rebalancing; measure throughput impact.
3) Trace p99 runs with tracing enabled + heap snapshot to confirm GC contribution. Narrowed to 30 p99 samples across runs.
4) Cost sim: plug measured GPU seconds into current pricing to estimate dollars per 1k tenants.

Hypotheses to validate:
- H1: adaptive TTL that lengthens for long-tail tenants (with sparse but stable pattern) reduces P95 by >40% vs fixed 60s without >10% increase in memory use.
- H2: sticky=on reduces misses by ~factor 4 for 30s cadence but will reduce cluster fairness during global load spikes.

Operational considerations / product notes:
- For hosted API: expose a tenant-level "keep-warm" opt-in where customers can request small persistent cache slots (metered). This could be cheaper than reserving dedicated capacity for sparse workloads.
- For Dedicated: offer a lightweight 'tiny hot pool' option per tenant (very small memory + 1 worker slot) that is cheaper than full dedicated. Could be a product toggle.

Log snippets (representative):
- 2026-02-25T09:12:04 INFO request-id=abc123 first_token_ms=612 cache_hit=false worker=gw-17
- 2026-02-25T09:12:35 INFO request-id=abc124 first_token_ms=420 cache_hit=true worker=gw-17
- 2026-02-25T10:22:10 WARN request-id=abc999 first_token_ms=6102 cache_hit=false worker=gw-17 (OOM-probe)

Quick TODOs in order of priority:
- [ ] Run p99 tracing pass and tag samples (Noah)
- [ ] Prototype adaptive TTL heuristic (Riley)
- [ ] Small A/B with sticky-lite=60s on 2 test tenants overnight (Ivy)
- [ ] Add metric for 'miss-led first-token penalty' to dashboard and alert when >10% for a tenant over 1h

Notes to self:
- Consider interplay with batching: glacial arrivals don't benefit from batching but keep-alive/slot retention might. Need to simulate multi-tenant mixture (many glacial tenants + occasional bursters) before shipping TTL defaults.
- Conversation with product: propose 'keep-warm slot' as add-on; quantify expected monthly cost vs customer SLA needs.

Bottom line (working):
- For sparse traffic, increasing KV TTL from 15s to ~60-300s or adding stickiness dramatically reduces tail latencies and wasted GPU time. Operational tradeoffs (memory and fairness) are manageable with caps and eviction policies. Next step: run adaptive TTL prototype and short sticky-lite A/B to get actionable numbers for product and infra decisions.

End of scratchpad.
